clue.text: History master's collection of Tudor hose

indicators.note: a collection is a gathering together of things in any order, so the letters that follow are reassembled

blocks.note: the nine letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A history teacher shows off his collection of Tudor stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: HERODOTUS, the Greek writer of the fifth century BC, is called the father of history.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek author is traditionally honoured as the first great historian, a master of that subject.

clue.text: .Book whose author conceals it

indicators.note: the phrase whose author is said to conceal the answer, which sits hidden across its words

blocks.note: found running from the end of whose into the start of author

explanation.surface: A book whose writer keeps something secret.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of HOSEA is named after the prophet held to be its author, so the clue also reads as a description of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosea is one of the books of the Old Testament, among the minor prophets of the Bible.

clue.text: Given a hot time by the critics

definitions.text: Given a hot time by the critics

blocks.note: surface reading: someone has had a warm, uncomfortable experience, or meat has been in an oven
setter's reading: critics who savage a play or book are said to give it a hot time

explanation.walkthrough: The word for cooking in an oven is also slang for being severely criticised, so both halves point to the same answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be roasted is informal for being harshly criticised or mocked, as well as cooked in dry heat.

clue.text: Taking away from Holmes's achievement

blocks.note: first meaning: subtraction, removing an amount
second meaning: Sherlock Holmes was famous for reasoning his way to conclusions

explanation.surface: Something is being subtracted from the great detective's success.
explanation.definitionFit: A deduction is both an amount subtracted and a conclusion reached by logical reasoning, the detective's speciality.

clue.text: Old-fashioned verdict on this paper in New York

definitions.note: the answer is a place in New York, so the definition is locative

blocks.note: the puzzle appears in The Times, so this paper is that newspaper
square is slang for conventional and out of date

explanation.surface: Someone judges this newspaper stuffy, while it is on sale in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The verdict on the paper is that it is square; in a down clue that word sits on, below, the paper's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Times Square is the famous busy intersection in Manhattan, a well-known location in New York.

clue.text: The drink that hardly ever made Corcoran sick

definitions.text: The drink that hardly ever made Corcoran sick

blocks.note: surface reading: some alcoholic beverage that rarely upset a man named Corcoran
setter's reading: Captain Corcoran in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore boasts he is never sick on the ocean, then admits: hardly ever

explanation.walkthrough: The drink is slang for the ocean. HMS Pinafore is a comic opera whose captain claims never to be seasick.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors and others call the ocean the drink, as in falling into the drink.

clue.text: Son in time of prosperity goes bust

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is put inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a boom is a period of economic growth
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A son goes bankrupt just when the economy is thriving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes bust' reads as financial ruin, but bust is the noun for the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosom is a woman's chest, and bust is a synonym for that part of the body.

clue.text: Transported second circular letter from island

indicators.note: something taken from a word is removed out of it

blocks.note: the large island in South-East Asia
O is round in shape; the island's name has two, and this is the latter one

explanation.surface: Someone was moved a second time by a round letter sent from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like it means S or a moment, but it chooses which O to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: Borne is the past participle of bear, meaning carried, so it matches transported.

clue.text: Boys who sing so quietly to queen

blocks.note: taken as written
P is piano, the musical direction for softly
a rani is an Indian queen

explanation.surface: Choirboys sing softly to the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural soprani is the Italian form; trebles in a choir are often boys singing the soprano part.
explanation.definitionFit: Soprani are singers of the highest vocal part, which in church choirs is sung by boy trebles.

clue.text: Rude mechanics -a bad lot

indicators.note: something rude is rough and unrefined, so the letters are knocked into a new shape

blocks.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's rude mechanicals, the amateur actors in A Midsummer Night's Dream, are a hopeless bunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bad lot' looks like a judgement on the workmen, but lot means fortune here.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischance is a piece of bad luck, and one's lot is one's fate or fortune.

clue.text: Fame achieved late by Andromeda

blocks.note: surface reading: someone became a celebrity only late in life
setter's reading: in Greek myth Andromeda was set among the stars as a constellation after her death

explanation.walkthrough: Andromeda became a group of stars, so she literally reached the condition of being a star, but only late.
explanation.definitionFit: Stardom is the status of being a celebrated star, which is to say great fame.

clue.text: A supporter, backed so pertinently

indicators.note: backed means sent backwards, so the short word after it is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
a prop holds something up
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A supporter backed someone's case, and did so to the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos is an adverb meaning appropriately or to the point, with relevance to the matter at hand.

clue.text: A tease, I see, as pronounced in old dialect

indicators.note: the words are to be taken as they sound when spoken, not as spelt

blocks.note: tease sounds like Ts, two letter Ts, and I see sounds like the letters I and C

explanation.surface: Someone spots a joker and comments on it in an old-fashioned accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken aloud, the phrase spells out the answer letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic Greek was the classical dialect of ancient Athens and its region, Attica.

clue.text: One at home in castle for Scottish callers

definitions.text: One at home in castle for Scottish callers

blocks.note: surface reading: a laird or resident living in a Scottish castle
setter's reading: the saying goes that an Englishman's home is his castle, and Scots call an Englishman by a particular name

explanation.walkthrough: Callers means people who call someone a name, not visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassenach is the Scottish, often mildly scornful, name for an English person.

clue.text: Cross man doesn't quite finish the course

indicators.note: not quite finishing means stopping just short, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: St Andrews in Scotland is the famous home of golf, with its Old Course

explanation.surface: An angry golfer gives up before completing the round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is the diagonal cross of the Scottish flag, named after its patron saint.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle was crucified on a diagonal cross, so the saltire is called his cross.

clue.text: Was obliged to give hothead notice

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the word splits as hot plus head, and the head of hot is its opening letter
an ad is a notice in a paper

explanation.surface: Someone was forced to dismiss a hothead from their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' looks like one word for a rash person, but it splits into hot and head.
explanation.definitionFit: Had to do something means was obliged to do it, so had alone stands for was obliged.

clue.text: Do fellows get fed up here?

definitions.text: Do fellows get fed up here?

blocks.note: surface reading: are people getting bored or annoyed
setter's reading: college fellows eat at a raised dining table above the students

explanation.walkthrough: Fellows of an Oxford or Cambridge college dine on a platform at the end of the hall, so they are fed up high.
explanation.definitionFit: In a college hall the raised table where senior members and guests dine is given this name.

clue.text: Such grilling often led to awful steak, it's said

definitions.text: Such grilling often led to awful steak, it's said

blocks.clueFragment: Such grilling often led to awful steak
blocks.note: surface reading: careless cooking spoils a piece of meat

blocks.clueFragment: grilling often led to awful steak, it's said
blocks.note: setter's reading: harsh questioning by a church tribunal often ended with heretics burned at a post that sounds like steak

explanation.walkthrough: Grilling is intense interrogation; steak, said aloud, is the stake of burning at the stake.
explanation.definitionFit: The historical church tribunal against heresy, and any harsh questioning, goes by this name.

clue.text: Looking undistinguished in uniform

blocks.note: surface reading: someone appears ordinary or unremarkable
setter's reading: people dressed the same cannot be told apart from one another

explanation.walkthrough: Undistinguished usually means mediocre, but here it means not distinguishable from each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are exactly alike in appearance cannot be told apart, which is what the answer describes.

clue.text: Enlargement ordered for novel title

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so the letters are put into a fresh sequence

blocks.note: the eleven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A photographic blow-up has been ordered for the title page of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Greenmantle is John Buchan's 1916 spy novel featuring Richard Hannay.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a well-known adventure book by Buchan, so it is a title of a novel.

clue.text: Quit with zero capital in this country

blocks.note: surface reading: someone leaves having scored nothing
setter's reading: the word quit with an O for zero added makes Quito, the capital of the country required

explanation.surface: Someone departed penniless, with no money left in this country.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like money, but it means a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Quito is the capital of this South American nation on the equator, so it is the country described.

clue.text: Signal to player, possibly needing support of rest

blocks.note: first meaning: the line or action that tells an actor to come in
second meaning: in snooker the stick may be laid on a rest, a support for awkward shots

explanation.walkthrough: A rest in snooker is a stick with a cross-shaped head used to steady the shot when the ball is out of reach.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the prompt for an actor's entrance and the stick used in billiards and snooker.

clue.text: Insular source of Dutch courage

blocks.note: surface reading: a narrow-minded origin of something
setter's reading: Dutch courage is drink-fuelled bravery, and the orange liqueur is named after a Dutch Caribbean island

explanation.walkthrough: Insular means of an island, not narrow-minded; and the island is Dutch, which literalises the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Curaçao is both an island of the Dutch Caribbean and the liqueur flavoured with oranges grown there.

clue.text: Bit of wood, perhaps, drawn by Constable

definitions.text: Bit of wood, perhaps, drawn by Constable

blocks.clueFragment: Bit of wood, perhaps, drawn by Constable
blocks.note: surface reading: John Constable, the English landscape painter, sketched part of a wood
setter's reading: a police constable draws a wooden club from its holder

explanation.walkthrough: The capital C makes Constable the painter; drawn means pulled out, not sketched.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is the short wooden club carried by British police officers.

clue.text: Men of this bunch in church

definitions.note: the answer completes the phrase men of the ___, meaning clergy

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: CH is the usual abbreviation for church
a lot is a group or set

explanation.surface: A group of men is gathered in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Men of the cloth are clergymen.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy are called men of the cloth, the phrase referring to clerical dress.

clue.text: Cast finished, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the word is taken as spoken

blocks.note: finished means through, as in I'm through

explanation.surface: The actors are done, we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast looks like a theatre company, but it is the past tense of the verb to cast.
explanation.definitionFit: Threw is the past tense of throw, and cast is a synonym meaning tossed.

clue.text: What is cut by the middle of September?

definitions.text: What is cut by the middle of September?

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, the only one kept
a word cut by something is split open with it lodged inside

blocks.note: taken as written
the fifth of its nine letters

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what gets harvested by mid-autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the grain crop is harvested by mid-September.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat is the cereal harvested in late summer, so it is a crop cut by the middle of September.

clue.text: Some support after retiring for our confidant

indicators.note: after places one piece later than the other in the word

blocks.note: retiring for the night means going to bed
a post is an upright support

explanation.surface: Someone finds support after going to bed for their confidant.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'between you and me and the bedpost' makes the bedpost a sharer of secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret said to be between you, me and the bedpost is told in confidence, so the post is a confidant.

clue.text: Fashion of the century

blocks.note: first meaning: style or fashionable society
second meaning: slang for a hundred, as a century of runs in cricket or 100 mph

explanation.surface: The style that defines an era.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means fashionable style and is also informal for a hundred of anything, such as a hundred runs.

clue.text: Convert in the case of the Ring, perhaps

blocks.note: re means concerning or with regard to
Wagner's Ring is a cycle of four operas; perhaps marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A change of heart in the matter of Wagner's operas.
explanation.walkthrough: Convert looks like a noun for a new believer, but it is the verb meaning to reprocess waste.
explanation.definitionFit: To recycle is to process used materials into something reusable, which is converting them.

clue.text: Very high cost of terminal

blocks.note: first meaning: something expensive costs the planet, an idiom for a huge price
second meaning: the electrical connection to ground

explanation.surface: An airport building costs a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Terminal suggests an airport, but it is an electrical contact.
explanation.definitionFit: Costing the earth is an idiom for being very expensive, and the earth wire or terminal grounds a circuit.

clue.text: Poles went astray at end of flight

indicators.note: something that goes astray wanders off course, so the letters scatter into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Polish travellers lost their way when their plane landed.
explanation.walkthrough: Went does double duty in the surface, but its letters belong to the fodder; flight means a flight of stairs, not air travel.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel post is the upright at the top or bottom of a staircase, supporting the handrail.
